no-priors.name: No Priors
no-priors.bio: Podcast: Biohub: The Future of Biology is Open-Source with Co-Founders Mark Zuckerberg, Priscilla Chan, and Head of Science Alex Rives

html_en:
From biology labs to boardrooms, this week's developments underscore a fundamental truth: we're witnessing the transition from experimental AI to infrastructure-dependent reality, where regulatory decisions and tool-building choices will shape entire industries.

The New Model Supply Chain Economics

Box CEO Aaron Levie delivered perhaps the most insightful analysis of where the AI industry is heading with his observations on model routing. He argues that
"The layer that can route to the best AI model for the particular job is going to increase in value substantially"
for three critical reasons: cost optimization, capability maximization, and risk mitigation. This isn't just theoretical optimization—it's becoming essential infrastructure. As Levie notes,
"despite the bitter lesson and models generally getting better in the same direction, there are still lots of differences between models. Some are better at tool use, others better at coding, and others again better at certain domains of knowledge work."
The timing couldn't be more prescient given recent regulatory turbulence. The intelligence routing layer may become the most valuable piece of AI infrastructure precisely because it offers flexibility in an increasingly uncertain regulatory landscape.

Regulatory Reality Check: The Fable Warning Shot

The sudden restriction of Anthropic's newest model sent shockwaves through the community, with Replit's Amjad Masad sensing something larger at play:
"Feels like we're getting psyoped. The end-game here is something bigger."
Levie provided crucial context, arguing this event is "actually net positive to regulation discourse" because it reveals what AI regulation would look like at scale:
"The government would have sole discretion over when a model can be released to the public, based on a bunch of factors that they inherently control... The net result is that we would end up with backlog of AI releases, progress in the market inherently would dramatically slow down."
Garry Tan captured the broader implications perfectly:
"I wish the significance of the model came from more people actually using it and coming to their own conclusions. But yes most people in the world learn about it through signifiers and not through interacting with that which is signified."

The Open Source Biology Moonshot

While AI models face regulatory headwinds, Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan are doubling down on open science with their $500 million commitment to virtual biology. In a fascinating No Priors podcast episode, they outlined their philosophy:
"We'll have a bigger impact by getting us in more scientists hands quicker by doing it as open source projects instead. It's not just like there's some factory somewhere that you can pay to produce the data. You actually need to invent new novel scientific approaches."
What's particularly striking is their data strategy. Unlike language models that can scrape the internet, biological AI requires creating entirely new datasets:
"Unlike language models, there's just like a lot of data out there on the Internet. That's not really the case with biology... a lot of the stuff that I think we wanna put into this, it doesn't exist."
Their Biohub has already folded over 1.1 billion proteins and predicted their structures, demonstrating the power of general biological models rather than narrow, application-specific ones.

The Ground Truth Builders

Perhaps the most telling moment of the week came from the trenches: Stefan Ceriu casually mentioning that he "got a PayPal verification text and thought I been hacked, but it was just codex signing up for a web service it needed." This isn't a demo or a benchmark—it's AI agents autonomously navigating real-world services, complete with verification flows. Garry Tan summed up the moment we're in:
"In AI most people are still trying to use old maps on a new territory. Throw the maps away. It's time to draw new ones. The only way you can do it is walking the land."
The future belongs to those building tools, routing intelligence efficiently, and creating new data rather than those debating capabilities from the sidelines. The infrastructure players are quietly positioning themselves to win the next phase of this transformation.
html_zh:
AI 行业正在经历一个监管与开放之间的微妙平衡时刻，而 Mark Zuckerberg 和 Priscilla Chan 对生物学的新承诺或许为我们展示了未来技术发展的另一种可能性。

AI 监管的分水岭时刻

Fable 模型被政府暂停发布的事件引发了科技界对 AI 监管未来的深度思考。Box CEO Aaron Levie 在一系列推文中提供了最为深刻的分析：
这整个 Fable 出口管制情况实际上对监管讨论是有正面意义的。这让我们提前看到了如果 AI 监管在模型层面而非特定应用层面实施时会是什么样子。政府将对模型何时可以向公众发布拥有绝对裁量权，基于他们本质上控制的一系列因素。
Levie 进一步警告说，这种监管模式可能会导致严重后果：
最终结果是我们会遇到 AI 发布的积压，市场进展本质上会大幅放缓，AI 将开始看起来像任何其他硬化的行业。如果这种模式在当前 AI 浪潮开始的三年前就存在，我们现在很可能仍然停留在 GPT-4 级别的智能水平。
与此同时，Replit 的 Amjad Masad 则对整个情况表示了怀疑："感觉我们正在被心理操作。这里的终局是更大的事情。"

模型路由：AI 基础设施的新前沿

Aaron Levie 在另一个引人深思的 推文串 中指出了 AI 基础设施发展的一个关键趋势：
能够为特定工作路由到最佳 AI 模型的层级价值将大幅增加。至少有三个重要原因：成本优化、能力最大化和风险缓解。
这种观点反映了一个日益重要的现实：随着不同模型在不同任务上展现出各自的优势，智能路由将成为应用 AI 层的战略优势。

开源生物学的宏伟愿景

在 No Priors 播客的一期特殊节目中，Mark Zuckerberg、Priscilla Chan 和 Alex Rives 深入讨论了他们 5 亿美元的虚拟生物学倡议。
我们只是想为整个科学界提供工具。
Zuckerberg 解释道。 Chan 补充说：
我们想了解生物学是如何工作的。我想了解这个人的基因学。我想了解他们对不同疾病的风险。我的目标是能够将个体作为个体来治疗，理解机制，并能够进行干预。
特别引人注目的是他们对开源方法的承诺：
通过将其作为开源项目更快地交到更多科学家手中，我们将产生更大的影响。这不仅仅是在某个地方有工厂可以付费生产数据。你实际需要发明新的新颖科学方法。
观看完整播客：Biohub: The Future of Biology is Open-Source

开发者社区的真实体验

在更实际的层面上，开发者们正在分享他们与新 AI 工具的真实体验。@thsottiaux 发推说："嗨，我是 Tibo，我刚发现了 Codex。有什么问题尽管问。"这条推文获得了超过 1400 个赞，显示了社区对新 AI 工具的巨大兴趣。 更有趣的是，@steipete 分享了一个意外的体验：
收到了 PayPal 验证短信，以为被黑客攻击了，但原来只是 codex 为它需要的网络服务注册。
这些真实的用户体验故事揭示了 AI 代理如何开始在开发者的日常工作流程中发挥越来越重要的作用。

新领域需要新地图

Initialized Capital 的 Garry Tan 为整个行业的现状提供了一个诗意的总结：
在 AI 领域，大多数人仍在试图在新领域使用旧地图。扔掉地图吧。是时候绘制新的了。唯一的方法就是走遍这片土地。
这种观点与@swyx 正在进行的 AI 工程调查形成了有趣的呼应，该调查旨在更好地了解这个快速发展的社区。正如 swyx 所说：
我们让 @devinai 分析了注册参会者名单，并输出了一个关于两周后来参加会议的人员的实时图表。这最终成为我见过的关于我们正在聚集什么样的社区的最佳数据驱动讲述。
随着 AI 行业在监管不确定性中继续快速发展，一件事变得清晰：无论是在生物学、软件开发还是监管政策方面，我们确实需要新的地图来导航这个勇敢的新世界。
